text: The LORD appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day.
He looked up and saw three men standing nearby. When he saw them, he ran from the tent entrance to meet them and bowed to the ground.
"My lord," he said, "if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant.
Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest under the tree.
Let me bring a piece of bread to refresh you, and then go on your way—since you have come by your servant." "Very well," they said, "do as you have said."
Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah. "Quick," he said, "three measures of the finest flour! Knead it and bake bread." [footnote: About twenty liters.]

versions.text: Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah. "Quick," he said, "three measures of the finest flour! Knead it and bake bread."
versions.explanation: A brief footnote on the quantity (three seahs) would help hearers grasp the lavishness of Abraham's hospitality without altering the readable text.

text: Then he ran to the herd, took a choice, tender calf, and gave it to his servant, who hurried to prepare it.
He took curds and milk and the calf that had been prepared, and set it all before them, and he stood by them under the tree while they ate.

versions.text: He took curds and milk and the calf that had been prepared and set it before them, and he stood by them under the tree while they ate.
versions.explanation: The singular pronoun "it" does not agree with the compound object (curds, milk, and the calf). A plural "them" is required, and a comma before "and set" helps the oral rhythm.

versions.text: He took curds and milk and the calf that had been prepared, and set them before them; and he stood by them under the tree while they ate.
versions.explanation: "set them before them" places two forms of "them" back to back, which stumbles when read aloud; "it all" keeps the plural sense of the compound object without the echo. Replacing the semicolon with a comma also smooths the oral rhythm of the closing clause.

text: They asked him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" "There, in the tent," he said.
Then he said, "I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife will have a son." Now Sarah was listening at the entrance of the tent, behind him.
Abraham and Sarah were old, well along in years, and Sarah was long past childbearing.
So Sarah laughed to herself and thought, "Now that I am worn out, am I to have pleasure? And my husband is old."
But the LORD said to Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh and say, 'Can I really bear a child, now that I am old?'
Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, about this time next year, and Sarah will have a son."
Sarah denied it: "I did not laugh"—for she was afraid. But he said, "Yes, you did laugh."
Then the men got up to leave and looked down toward Sodom, and Abraham walked along with them to see them on their way.
And the LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?
Abraham will surely become a great and mighty nation, and through him all the nations of the earth will be blessed.

For I have chosen him, so that he will direct his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just, so that the LORD may bring about for Abraham what he has promised him."
Then the LORD said, "The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and their sin is very grave.
I will go down now and see whether they have acted as badly as the outcry that has reached me. If not, I will know.

versions.text: I will go down and see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me. If not, I will know."
versions.explanation: "done altogether according to the outcry" is stilted and hard to follow when read aloud; the suggested wording keeps the sense of כָּלָה (utterly/completely) while flowing more naturally, and renders the softening particle נָּא.

text: The men turned from there and went toward Sodom, but Abraham remained standing before the LORD.
Then Abraham came near and said, "Will you really sweep away the righteous with the wicked?
Suppose there are fifty righteous people in the city. Will you really sweep it away and not spare the place for the sake of the fifty righteous who are in it?
Far be it from you to do such a thing—to kill the righteous with the wicked, treating the righteous and the wicked alike! Far be it from you! Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?"
The LORD said, "If I find fifty righteous people in the city of Sodom, I will spare the whole place for their sake."
Abraham answered, "Now that I have ventured to speak to the Lord, though I am but dust and ashes—
suppose the fifty righteous are five short. Will you destroy the whole city because of five?" "If I find forty-five there," he said, "I will not destroy it."
Abraham spoke to him again: "What if only forty are found there?" He said, "For the sake of the forty, I will not do it."

versions.text: Abraham spoke to him again: "Suppose only forty are found there?" He said, "For the sake of the forty, I will not do it."
versions.explanation: "Suppose ... ?" is a statement punctuated as a question. "What if ...?" is a genuine interrogative and reads more naturally aloud. (The same adjustment could be applied consistently in the following pleas.)

text: Then he said, "May the Lord not be angry, but let me speak. Suppose only thirty are found there?" He answered, "If I find thirty there, I will not do it."
He said, "Now that I have ventured to speak to the Lord, suppose only twenty are found there?" He said, "For the sake of the twenty, I will not destroy it."
Then he said, "May the Lord not be angry, but let me speak just once more. Suppose only ten are found there?" He answered, "For the sake of the ten, I will not destroy it."
When the LORD had finished speaking with Abraham, he went on his way, and Abraham returned home.
